analysis.one_liner: Requires three-judge panels for nationwide court orders and random judge assignment to stop venue shopping.
analysis.headline: The Fair Courts Act died in the Senate Judiciary Committee with no hearing, no vote, and zero cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would make it much harder for a lawsuit filer to steer a case to a single friendly judge and win a ruling that blocks a federal policy nationwide. It bars a lone district judge from issuing nationwide injunctions, orders vacating federal regulations nationwide, or stays of those orders unless a panel of three district judges hears the case [S2][S3]. It also requires courts to randomly assign cases so no single judge has more than a 25% chance of drawing any given case, and to publish their case-assignment rules online [S2][S3].
analysis.who_benefits: Anyone who depends on federal rules — workers, consumers, patients, and the agencies that enforce those rules — gains, because no single hand-picked judge could halt a national policy with one order. It also protects everyone from the reverse scenario: any group, whatever its politics, would lose the ability to pick its judge. Well-funded litigants who currently exploit the system lose their advantage; ordinary litigants, who rarely have a choice of forum, are barely affected in that respect.

how_it_helps.text: A single district judge could no longer issue a nationwide injunction against the federal government, vacate a federal regulation nationwide, or stay such relief — those orders would require a three-judge district court panel [S2][S3].

District courts would have to randomly assign cases so the chance of drawing any particular judge stays at or below 25%, closing the main route to filing suit in a one-judge division chosen for its likely ruling [S2][S3].
District courts would have to publish their case-division orders on their websites, making it publicly visible how cases are routed to judges [S2][S3].
The bill states it does not expand or limit the forms of relief courts may grant — it changes who can issue them and how cases are assigned, not the underlying law [S3].

analysis.who_pays: If it passed, the cost would fall on well-funded litigants and interest groups that shop for favorable judges — they would lose their best tool for overturning or blocking federal rules with a single ruling. All litigants seeking nationwide relief would face a heavier, slower three-judge process, and courts in small districts would need to borrow judges from neighboring districts to meet the random-assignment rule.
analysis.who_pays_short: Lawsuit filers who pick favorable judges

drawbacks.text: The rules would bind everyone, not just the groups the bill targets: civil-rights, consumer, and progressive litigants who sometimes obtain nationwide relief from friendly judges would also need a three-judge panel, and such panels add time and cost to litigation [S3].

Random assignment and three-judge panels would complicate case management, especially in low-population districts with few judges, which would have to draw on judges from adjacent districts in the same state to comply [S3].

The bill addresses judge and venue shopping but not the underlying demand: well-resourced parties could still file repeated, strategically framed challenges to federal actions in courts generally viewed as favorable, just spread across a panel.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real and broad: national policy would no longer hinge on one district judge drawn from a hand-picked courthouse, a practice that has let well-funded challengers freeze federal rules nationwide. The costs are mostly procedural — slower relief, heavier panels, administrative complexity in small districts — and the same restraints apply to plaintiffs of every political leaning, which is the honest trade-off any anti-forum-shopping rule carries. On balance the bill's design is sound; the deeper problem it only partly addresses is how much resource-intensive litigation shapes national policy.

outcome.mechanism: Wyden introduced the bill and it sat in the Senate Judiciary Committee — no hearing, no markup, no vote — until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Wyden introduced the bill on May 30, 2023, and it was read twice and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee [S1][S5].
No senator from either party signed on as a cosponsor [S4].
The action record shows nothing after the committee referral; the bill never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Litigants with the resources to shop for a favorable judge — including industry and ideological groups that file challenges to federal rules — keep the current system, where a single chosen judge can block a national policy.

for.name: Ron Wyden
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Fair Courts Act of 2023 to curb venue shopping; the bill had no other Senate support and went no further.

against.name: Dick Durbin
against.what_they_did: The committee the bill was referred to never held a hearing or markup on it; the bill sat there until the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken, and the bill's only support was its Democratic sponsor — zero cosponsors from either party — so its partisan shape was never tested.

industries.industry: Business and ideological litigation groups that challenge federal rules
industries.note: These groups — trade associations, state-aligned challengers, and advocacy litigation shops — currently can file in a single-judge division chosen for its likely outcome and win a nationwide ruling against a federal regulation. The bill would force such cases before a randomly drawn three-judge panel, raising the bar for nationwide relief.
Agencies would be far less exposed to a single judge vacating their rules nationwide, letting worker, consumer, and health protections stay in effect while cases proceed.

industries.industry: Law firms specializing in regulatory challenges
industries.note: Firms whose business model rests on steering high-stakes federal challenges to favorable districts would lose that edge, though the same firms litigate on both sides and could adapt to three-judge panels.
